l: Fravashis of the saints, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments, The Gâhs. / I. The Gâh Hâvan. .. V. Gâh Ushahin.
s: The Fravashis of the saints receive sacrifice and homage as the good, heroic, and bountiful Fravashis of saints, including those of the living, the dead, the bodily, and those in heaven. They are also invoked in connection with the holy woman, prosperity, and the good order.

l: the five Gâthas, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments, The Gâhs. / I. The Gâh Hâvan. .. V. Gâh Ushahin.
s: The five Gâthas are described as a surpassing Mãthra invoked through Airyemâ-ishyô. The Gâh Rapithvin names the Gâthas Ahunavaiti, Ustavaiti, Spentâ-mainyu, Vohu-khshathra, and Vahistôisti as holy and ruling in the ritual order.

l: Fire, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments, The Gâhs. / I. The Gâh Hâvan. .. V. Gâh Ushahin.
s: Fire is repeatedly called Ahura Mazda's son and the holy lord of the ritual order. It receives sacrifice, homage, propitiation, praise, and blessing, and is associated with Asha Vahista.

l: Apãm-napât, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments, The Gâhs. / I. The Gâh Hâvan. .. V. Gâh Ushahin.
s: Apãm-napât is invoked as a lofty and royal Ahura associated with the waters created by Mazda. He is described as brilliant and having fleet horses, and receives sacrifice, homage, propitiation, praise, and blessing.

l: Righteousness the Best, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments, The Gâhs. / I. The Gâh Hâvan. .. V. Gâh Ushahin.
s: Asha Vahista is identified with Righteousness the Best and is repeatedly propitiated and sacrificed to. She is associated with Ahura Mazda's Fire and receives blessing for sacrifice, homage, strength, and swiftness.

l: Zantuma, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments, The Gâhs. / I. The Gâh Hâvan. .. V. Gâh Ushahin.
s: Zantuma is named as a holy lord of the ritual order alongside Frâdat-fshu. Sacrifice is offered to him and for his worship and homage, including in connection with the assembly of the Bountiful Immortals.

l: Dahvyuma, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments, The Gâhs. / I. The Gâh Hâvan. .. V. Gâh Ushahin.
s: Dahvyuma is named as a holy lord of the ritual order alongside Frâdat-vîra. Sacrifice is offered to him in connection with the manifest performance and fulfillment of truth, later lore, and the creation by day and night.

l: Sraosha, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments, The Gâhs. / I. The Gâh Hâvan. .. V. Gâh Ushahin.
s: Sraosha is called Obedience and is described as blessed, endowed with recompense or sanctity, smiting with the blow of victory, and causing settlements to advance and increase. He receives sacrifice and blessing in Gâh Ushahin.

l: Rashnu, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments, The Gâhs. / I. The Gâh Hâvan. .. V. Gâh Ushahin.
s: Rashnu is described as the most just. He receives sacrifice in Gâh Ushahin and is included in the final blessing of sacrifice, homage, strength, and swiftness.

l: Arstât, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments, The Gâhs. / I. The Gâh Hâvan. .. V. Gâh Ushahin.
s: Arstât is described as causing the settlements to advance and increase. He receives sacrifice and is included with Sraosha and Rashnu in the final blessing.

l: Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments, Miscellaneous Fragments. / I. .. IX.
s: The Miscellaneous Fragments contain ritual instructions, praises, confessions, prayers, and teachings concerning Mazda-worship, sacrifice, moral conduct, and cosmic order. Zarathustra Spitama is instructed to declare words for worship, while Ahura Mazda, the Bountiful Immortals, waters, plants, Fravashis, and Yazads receive praise or sacrifice. The unit teaches that good thoughts, words, and deeds lead to Heaven, while evil ones lead to Hell, and it calls for the defeat of Angra Mainyu, the Daêvas, and the Drug(k). It also presents prayers and sacred words, including the Airyemâ-ishyô, Ahuna-vairya, Khshathra-vairya, Yâ daêna, and the Mãthra-spenta word, as powerful and victorious.

l: Miscellaneous Fragments, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments, Miscellaneous Fragments. / I. .. IX.
s: The Miscellaneous Fragments contain ritual directions, prayers, praises, confessions, moral teachings, and invocations concerning Mazda-worship and the defeat of evil.

l: Zarathustra, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments, Miscellaneous Fragments. / I. .. IX.
s: Zarathustra Spitama is told to declare words for sacrifice and worship to the male and female disciples of Zarathustra Spitama. He is also addressed in declarations concerning the Airyemâ-ishyô and the Drug(k).

l: Ahura Mazda, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments, Miscellaneous Fragments. / I. .. IX.
s: Ahura Mazda is praised as radiant and glorious, and sacrifices are offered to him. He declares that he will rule as sovereign over his creatures and that the Kingdom belongs to him.

l: Khshathra-vairya, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments, Miscellaneous Fragments. / I. .. IX.
s: Khshathra-vairya is named with the Good Mind and Righteousness the Best. It is also identified as the Kingdom to be desired and is invoked against the Drug(k).

l: the Bountiful Immortals, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments, Miscellaneous Fragments. / I. .. IX.
s: The Bountiful Immortals are invoked in ritual instruction and receive sacrifice. They are described as ruling and disposing of all things aright.

l: Thraêtaona, the Âthwyan, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments, Miscellaneous Fragments. / I. .. IX.
s: Thraêtaona, the Âthwyan, is praised and worshipped as a saint and holy lord of the ritual order. Propitiation, sacrifice, homage, strength, and swiftness are offered to his Fravashi.

l: Heaven, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments, Miscellaneous Fragments. / I. .. IX.
s: Heaven is described as the home of those who think good thoughts, speak good words, and do good deeds. It is called the best world.

l: Hell, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments, Miscellaneous Fragments. / I. .. IX.
s: Hell is identified as the place where those who think, speak, and do evil thoughts, words, and deeds abide.

l: good thoughts, words, and deeds, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments, Miscellaneous Fragments. / I. .. IX.
s: Good thoughts, words, and deeds are performed with intelligence. Those who think, speak, and do them are assigned Heaven, the best world.

l: evil thoughts, words, and deeds, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments, Miscellaneous Fragments. / I. .. IX.
s: Evil thoughts, words, and deeds are performed with folly. Those who think, speak, and do them are assigned Hell.

l: Airyemâ-ishyô, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments, Miscellaneous Fragments. / I. .. IX.
s: The Airyemâ-ishyô is proclaimed the greatest, most influential, and most helpful of authoritative prayers. The Saoshyants are urged to use and revere it.

l: Angra Mainyu, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments, Miscellaneous Fragments. / I. .. IX.
s: Angra Mainyu is contrasted with Ahura Mazda as a ruler over realms. He is commanded to be hidden beneath the earth, and no one is to rule as Angra Mainyu over Ahura Mazda’s realms.

l: Daêvas, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments, Miscellaneous Fragments. / I. .. IX.
s: The Daêvas are commanded to disappear beneath the earth. Their disappearance is associated with the unhindered arising of the dead and the sustaining of bodily life.

l: Apãm-napât, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments, Miscellaneous Fragments. / I. .. IX.
s: Apãm-napât is addressed as the lofty lord of the waters. Sacrifice, homage, propitiation, and praise are offered to him.

l: Ahurian One of Ahura, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments, Miscellaneous Fragments. / I. .. IX.
s: The Ahurian One of Ahura is addressed as the water which Mazda created. Praises, sacrifices, deeds of adoration, and offerings are directed to this being.

l: Drug(k), Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments, Miscellaneous Fragments. / I. .. IX.
s: The Drug(k) is described as a malignant and sinful force that causes the moons of the season to wane. She advances with a weapon and great strength, but the text calls for her death and destruction.

l: Ahuna-vairya, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments, Miscellaneous Fragments. / I. .. IX.
s: The Ahuna-vairya is identified as a prayer to be revered and chosen as Mazda’s choice one. Its words are said to belong to Mazda and to be among the victorious sacred words.

l: Mãthra-spenta word, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments, Miscellaneous Fragments. / I. .. IX.
s: The Mãthra-spenta word is described as unsubdued, undeceived, victorious, opposed to malice, healing, and victorious. When pronounced, it gives great victory to the person who utters it.

l: Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Vendidad (Vendîdâd) / Fargard I.
s: Ahura Mazda tells Spitama Zarathustra that he created every land dear to its dwellers and describes the good lands and countries he made. The first sixteen lands include Airyana Vaêgô, the plains in Sughdha, the strong, holy Môuru, and the beautiful Bâkhdhi with high-lifted banners. Angra Mainyu counter-created harmful beings, sins, and conditions in each land, including the serpent in the river and winter in Airyana Vaêgô. The passage concludes that there are still other beautiful, desirable, and thriving lands and countries.

l: Ahura Mazda, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Vendidad (Vendîdâd) / Fargard I.
s: Ahura Mazda tells Spitama Zarathustra that he made every land dear to its dwellers. He created the good lands and countries described in the unit.

l: Zarathustra, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Vendidad (Vendîdâd) / Fargard I.
s: Spitama Zarathustra is addressed by Ahura Mazda, who tells him about the lands and countries that were created and the evils counter-created in them.

l: the good lands and countries, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Vendidad (Vendîdâd) / Fargard I.
s: The good lands and countries were created by Ahura Mazda, beginning with Airyana Vaêgô and continuing through sixteen named lands. They are described as beautiful, deep, desirable, bright, and thriving.

l: Airyana Vaêgô, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Vendidad (Vendîdâd) / Fargard I.
s: Airyana Vaêgô was the first of the good lands and countries created by Ahura Mazda, by the good river Dâitya. Angra Mainyu counter-created the serpent in the river and winter there, and it has ten winter months and two summer months.

l: Angra Mainyu, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Vendidad (Vendîdâd) / Fargard I.
s: Angra Mainyu, who is all death, counter-created harmful beings, sins, and conditions by his witchcraft in the lands made by Ahura Mazda. His counter-creations include the serpent in the river and winter in Airyana Vaêgô.

l: fatal winters, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Vendidad (Vendîdâd) / Fargard I.
s: Winter is described as a counter-creation of Angra Mainyu and a work of the Daêvas. In Airyana Vaêgô, there are ten winter months and two summer months, and winter falls with the worst of its plagues.

l: the plains in Sughdha, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Vendidad (Vendîdâd) / Fargard I.
s: The plains in Sughdha were the second of the good lands and countries created by Ahura Mazda. Angra Mainyu counter-created the fly Skaitya there, which brings death to the cattle.

l: the strong, holy Môuru, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Vendidad (Vendîdâd) / Fargard I.
s: The strong, holy Môuru was the third of the good lands and countries created by Ahura Mazda. Angra Mainyu counter-created sinful lusts there.

l: the beautiful Bâkhdhi with high-lifted banners, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Vendidad (Vendîdâd) / Fargard I.
s: The beautiful Bâkhdhi with high-lifted banners was the fourth of the good lands and countries created by Ahura Mazda. Angra Mainyu counter-created the Bravara there.

l: Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard II.
s: Zarathustra asks Ahura Mazda who first received the law of Ahura, and Ahura Mazda identifies Yima, who instead undertakes to nourish, rule, and watch over the material world. Under Yima’s rule, the earth becomes overcrowded, so he enlarges it three times. Ahura Mazda then warns Yima of fatal winters and commands him to build the Vara, where selected men and women, animals, plants, and fires will be preserved. The Vara is completed, has its own lights and inhabitants, and is ruled by Urvatad-nara and Zarathustra, while Karshipta brings the law of Mazda there.

l: Zarathustra, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard II.
s: Zarathustra asks Ahura Mazda about the first mortal taught the law of Ahura. He is identified as one of the rulers of the Vara together with Urvatad-nara.

l: Ahura Mazda, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard II.
s: Ahura Mazda teaches Yima the law of Ahura and instructs him to nourish, rule, and watch over the material world. He warns Yima about overcrowding and fatal winters, commands him to build the Vara, and answers questions about its lights, law, and ruler.

l: Yima, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard II.
s: Yima is the first mortal before Zarathustra to converse with Ahura Mazda and be taught the law of Ahura, but he declines to be its preacher and bearer. He enlarges the earth as it becomes overcrowded and builds the Vara to preserve selected life from the fatal winters.

l: law of Mazda, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard II.
s: The law of Ahura is taught by Ahura Mazda to Yima before Zarathustra. Yima does not accept the role of preacher and bearer of the law.

l: material world, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard II.
s: The material world is placed under Yima’s care, and Ahura Mazda warns that fatal winters will fall upon it. The winters will bring fierce frost, heavy snow, and the destruction of the three sorts of beasts.

l: Earth, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard II.
s: The earth becomes full of flocks, herds, men, dogs, birds, and red blazing fires under Yima’s rule. Yima makes it larger by one-third, then by two-thirds, and finally by three-thirds.

l: golden ring, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard II.
s: Ahura Mazda gives Yima a golden ring and a gold-inlaid poniard as signs of royal sway. Yima uses the golden ring to press and enlarge the earth, and later seals the Vara with it.

l: men, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard II.
s: Men are among the beings that multiply until there is no more room on the earth. Selected men are brought into the Vara, where they live the happiest life.

l: Airyana Vaêgô, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard II.
s: Airyana Vaêgô is the place where Ahura Mazda, by the good river Dâitya, calls together a meeting of the celestial gods. It is also where Yima calls together a meeting of the excellent mortals.

l: the good river Dâitya, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard II.
s: Dâitya is described as the good river by which Ahura Mazda and Yima call their respective meetings in Airyana Vaêgô.

l: fatal winters, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard II.
s: The fatal winters are foretold by Ahura Mazda as coming upon the material world. They bring fierce, foul frost and deep snow, causing the three sorts of beasts to perish.

l: Vara, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard II.
s: The Vara is a square enclosure built by Yima as an abode for men and a fold for flocks. It contains waters, birds, dwellings, selected seeds of living beings and plants, nine streets, a golden seal, a door, and a self-shining window.

l: men and women (Vara), Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard II.
s: The Vara receives seeds of men and women of the greatest, best, and finest kinds on earth. Every fortieth year, each couple has two children, a male and a female.

l: cattle, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard II.
s: Selected seeds of sheep, oxen, and every kind of cattle are brought into the Vara. The cattle remain there with the preserved men, women, plants, birds, and fires.

l: Angra Mainyu, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard II.
s: Angra Mainyu is associated with the brands that stamp the bodies of mortals. No such brands, nor the other listed defects and afflictions, are present in the Vara.

l: Karshipta, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard II.
s: Karshipta is the bird who brings the law of Mazda into the Vara made by Yima.

l: Urvatad-nara, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard II.
s: Urvatad-nara is named by Ahura Mazda as the lord and ruler in the Vara, together with Zarathustra.

l: Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard III.
s: Fargard III concerns the Earth and the teachings of Ahura Mazda to Zarathustra about what brings the Earth happiness or grief. The Earth is happiest where the faithful worship, build thriving households, cultivate land, increase herds, and produce dung, while it grieves over corpses, Dakhmas, fiendish burrows, and captive families. Ahura Mazda teaches rules concerning carrying and burying corpses, repentance, cultivation, eating, and giving to the faithful. The unit also describes the law of Mazda as cleansing confessed sins and removing their penalties.

l: Earth, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard III.
s: The Earth feels happiest where the faithful worship, establish thriving households, cultivate land, increase flocks and herds, and produce dung. It feels grief where fiends emerge, corpses are buried, Dakhmas stand, Angra Mainyu's creatures have burrows, or the families of the faithful are led into captivity. The Earth rejoices most when corpses are removed, Dakhmas are pulled down, fiendish burrows are filled, land is cultivated, and cultivated produce is kindly given to the faithful.

l: Ahura Mazda, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard III.
s: Ahura Mazda answers Zarathustra's questions about the Earth's happiness and grief, the treatment of corpses, cultivation, food, and sin. He teaches that sowing corn fulfills and strengthens the law of Mazda, and that the law of Mazda can cleanse confessed sin.

l: Zarathustra, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard III.
s: Zarathustra is addressed by Ahura Mazda as Spitama Zarathustra while receiving teachings about the Earth, cultivation, food, corpses, and the law of Mazda.

l: worshippers of Mazda, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard III.
s: The faithful worship with holy objects, establish houses with priests and thriving families and herds, cultivate the Earth, and may receive produce from those who till the land. The wife and children of a faithful person may be driven into captivity, and the faithful are among those from whom a corpse must be kept at prescribed distances.

l: law of Mazda, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard III.
s: The law of Mazda is fulfilled and strengthened through worship, sowing corn, and acts of holiness. It takes away the confessed sins of a person who acknowledges them and resolves not to repeat forbidden deeds, cleansing evil thoughts, words, and deeds.

l: corn, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard III.
s: Sowing corn is identified as the food that fulfills the law of Mazda and as an act that makes holiness and the law of Mazda grow. The growth of barley, corn, and wheat drives away and destroys the Daêvas, while a person who eats has strength for holiness, husbandry, and begetting children.

l: cultivation of the earth, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard III.
s: Cultivation involves tilling the Earth with the left and right arms, watering dry ground, drying wet ground, and growing corn, grass, and fruit. The Earth rewards the cultivator with people seeking bread and abundant food, while the uncultivated person must beg at a stranger's door.

l: burial of corpses, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard III.
s: A person who buries the corpse of a dog or a man must disinter it within the stated period or receive increasing stripes. Burial left until the second year has no payment, atonement, or cleansing when committed by a professor or student of the law of Mazda.

l: sin, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard III.
s: Sin may be removed when a person confesses it and resolves never to commit the forbidden deed again. The law of Mazda takes away many sins and penalties, including breach of trust, murdering one of the faithful, burying a corpse, and deeds for which there is no atonement.

l: Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard IV.
s: Fargard IV concerns contracts, their breach, assaults, atonement, and penalties. Ahura Mazda defines six contracts, explains how each is redeemed by a higher contract, and assigns escalating atonements and stripes for breaking them. It also classifies threatening or assaultive acts as Âgerepta, Avaoirista, or Aredus, with repeated or unatoned offenses making the offender a Peshôtanu. The unit further describes agreements involving goods, wives, and knowledge, and imposes severe punishment for knowingly lying before the truth-knowing water.

l: Fargard IV, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard IV.
s: Fargard IV sets out rules concerning contracts and outrages. It defines six contracts, prescribes penalties for breaking them, classifies violence and bodily assault, and describes severe punishments for repeated offenses and deliberate falsehood.

l: Ahura Mazda, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard IV.
s: Ahura Mazda identifies six contracts: the word-contract, hand-contract, sheep-contract, ox-contract, man-contract, and field-contract. He states the required atonements and stripe penalties for broken contracts, assaults, and knowingly lying before the truth-knowing water.

l: man (offender), Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard IV.
s: The man who keeps another's property after being asked to return it is said to steal and rob. A man who breaks contracts, commits assaults, refuses atonement, or knowingly lies may incur escalating stripes and become a Peshôtanu.

l: word-contract, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard IV.
s: The word-contract is the first and lowest of the six contracts. If broken, it is redeemed by the hand-contract, and the offender incurs a three hundred-fold atonement, three hundred stripes with the Aspahê-astra, and three hundred with the Sraoshô-karana.

l: hand-contract, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard IV.
s: The hand-contract is the second of the six contracts and redeems a broken word-contract. If broken, it is redeemed by the sheep-contract, with a six hundred-fold atonement and six hundred stripes with each of the Aspahê-astra and Sraoshô-karana.

l: sheep-contract, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard IV.
s: The sheep-contract is the third of the six contracts and redeems a broken hand-contract. If broken, it is redeemed by the ox-contract, with a seven hundred-fold atonement and seven hundred stripes with each instrument.

l: ox-contract, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard IV.
s: The ox-contract is the fourth of the six contracts and redeems a broken sheep-contract. If broken, it is redeemed by the man-contract, with an eight hundred-fold atonement and eight hundred stripes with each instrument.

l: man-contract, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard IV.
s: The man-contract is the fifth of the six contracts and redeems a broken ox-contract. If broken, it is redeemed by the field-contract, with a nine hundred-fold atonement and nine hundred stripes with each instrument.

l: field-contract, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard IV.
s: The field-contract is the sixth and highest contract, described as concerning a field in good, fruitful, and productive land. If broken, it carries a thousand-fold atonement and a thousand stripes with each of the Aspahê-astra and Sraoshô-karana.

l: contract-breaking, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard IV.
s: Breaking a contract makes the offender's Nabânazdistas answerable for an atonement whose amount increases from three hundred-fold for the word-contract to a thousand-fold for the field-contract. The corresponding stripe penalties likewise increase from three hundred to a thousand with each instrument.

l: atonement, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard IV.
s: A broken contract requires an atonement corresponding to its level, from three hundred-fold for the word-contract through a thousand-fold for the field-contract. Repeated assaults committed without atoning for preceding offenses, or committed with refusal to atone, result in Peshôtanu status and two hundred stripes with each instrument.

l: Aspahê-astra, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard IV.
s: The Aspahê-astra is used for the prescribed stripes. Penalties range from five stripes for a first Âgerepta to two hundred stripes for a Peshôtanu, and from three hundred to a thousand stripes for broken contracts.

l: Sraoshô-karana, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard IV.
s: The Sraoshô-karana is used alongside the Aspahê-astra for the prescribed stripes. The number of stripes matches the penalty assigned for contracts, Âgerepta, Avaoirista, Aredus, bodily assault, and deliberate falsehood.

l: Âgerepta, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard IV.
s: An Âgerepta occurs when a man rises up to smite another. Its penalties escalate from five stripes with each instrument on the first occurrence to ninety on the seventh; an eighth unatoned occurrence or refusal to atone makes the offender a Peshôtanu liable to two hundred stripes with each instrument.

l: Avaoirista, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard IV.
s: An Avaoirista occurs when a man comes upon another to smite him. Its penalties rise from ten stripes with each instrument on the first occurrence to ninety on the sixth; a seventh unatoned occurrence or refusal to atone makes the offender a Peshôtanu liable to two hundred stripes with each instrument.

l: Aredus, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard IV.
s: An Aredus occurs when a man actually smites another with evil aforethought. Its penalties rise from fifteen stripes with each instrument on the first occurrence to ninety on the fifth; a sixth unatoned occurrence or refusal to atone makes the offender a Peshôtanu liable to two hundred stripes with each instrument.

l: Peshôtanu, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard IV.
s: A Peshôtanu is the status assigned when specified assaults are repeated without atonement or when the offender refuses to atone. The penalty stated for this status is two hundred stripes with the Aspahê-astra and two hundred with the Sraoshô-karana.

l: violence and bodily assault, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard IV.
s: Violence is classified as Âgerepta, Avaoirista, or Aredus according to whether a man rises to strike, approaches to strike, or strikes with evil aforethought. Bodily assaults receive escalating penalties: striking and seriously hurting another, causing blood, breaking a bone, or causing death each leads to specified stripes, with repeated unatoned or refused offenses making the offender a Peshôtanu.

l: Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard V.
s: This unit concerns Ahura Mazda’s teachings to Zarathustra about corpses, death, water, fire, purity, and the law of Mazda and Zarathustra. It explains rules for handling corpses, dead matter, houses for the dead, Dakhmas, contaminated objects, and a still-born child. It describes the effects of the Drug Nasu on people and dogs, and the pollution caused by an Ashemaogha. It also teaches about the movement and cleansing of water and the greatness of purity and the law.

l: Ahura Mazda, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard V.
s: Ahura Mazda answers Zarathustra’s questions about corpses, dead matter, water, fire, purity, pollution, and the treatment of a still-born child. He teaches the rules for houses for the dead, Dakhmas, contaminated clothing, and the law of Mazda and Zarathustra.

l: Zarathustra, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard V.
s: Zarathustra asks Ahura Mazda about dead matter, water, fire, purity, pollution, and the treatment of corpses and a still-born child. Ahura Mazda addresses him as righteous Zarathustra and Spitama Zarathustra.

l: worshippers of Mazda, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard V.
s: The worshippers of Mazda must build houses for the dead, place corpses on the Dakhma, and follow prescribed periods and purification rules. They must also handle a still-born child and the mother according to the stated distances, foods, confinement, and washing requirements.

l: Drug Nasu, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard V.
s: The Drug Nasu rushes forth when a person or certain dogs die and defiles nearby beings according to the stated order. It does not defile any creature when an Urupi dog dies, except the person who smites and kills it.

l: sea Vouru-kasha, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard V.
s: The sea Vouru-kasha sends waters down with the wind and clouds to corpses, Dakhmas, unclean remains, and bones. The waters later return unseen from the sea Pûitika toward the well-watered tree.

l: sea Pûitika, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard V.
s: The sea Pûitika receives the returning waters, where they stand boiling and are cleansed. The cleansed waters then flow back to the sea Vouru-kasha.

l: Dakhma, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard V.
s: The Dakhma is the place where worshippers of Mazda lay down the dead with the eyes toward the sun. It is rained on while the corpse and unclean remains are exposed, and water flows down to it.

l: law of Mazda, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard V.
s: The law of Mazda procures purity for the person who cleanses the self with good thoughts, words, and deeds. It is described as a fiend-destroying law greater, better, and fairer than other utterances.

l: law of Zarathustra, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard V.
s: The law of Zarathustra is called a fiend-destroying law and is compared in greatness, goodness, and fairness to the sea Vouru-kasha, a great stream, a great tree, and heaven above earth. It allows specified remission or absolution through the Ratu, the Sraoshâ-varez, and repentance.

l: purity, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard V.
s: Purity is described as the greatest good for man next to life. It is procured by the law of Mazda through good thoughts, words, and deeds.

l: woman with child, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard V.
s: A woman with child who brings forth a still-born child must be placed in the cleanest and driest part of a Mazdean house, thirty paces from fire, water, and baresma and three paces from the faithful. She must drink gômêz mixed with ashes, remain on prescribed food and in confinement, and later wash her body and clothes with gômêz and water.

l: still-born child, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard V.
s: A still-born child is treated as requiring special separation and purification procedures for the woman who bears it. The text directs that the woman be established in an enclosure and kept apart for the stated periods.

l: Ashemaogha, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard V.
s: An Ashemaogha, while alive, directly and indirectly defiles the creatures of the good spirit by harming water, fire, the cow, and faithful people. When dead, he defiles no more than a frog whose venom is dried up and which has been dead for more than a year.

l: corpse, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard V.
s: A corpse may be carried by dogs, birds, wolves, winds, or flies without causing sin to the person where it arrives. Corpses are kept in houses for the dead and then laid on the Dakhma, where rain and birds act upon them.

l: water, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard V.
s: Water does not kill a man; Astô-vîdhôtu, Vaya, the flood, birds, and chance are described in connection with his death. Water flows to corpses, Dakhmas, unclean remains, and bones, then returns through the sea Pûitika after being cleansed.

l: Fire, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard V.
s: Fire does not kill a man; Astô-vîdhôtu and Vaya are described as carrying him off, after which fire burns up life and limb. Fire and the sacred objects must be removed from a house where a dog or man dies and may be brought back after the prescribed period.

l: Mazdean house, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard V.
s: A house containing the fire, baresma, cups, Haoma, and mortar must be cleared of those objects when a dog or man dies there. The fire may return after nine nights in winter or a month in summer, and a house with a woman who bears a still-born child must provide a clean enclosure at prescribed distances.

l: houses for the dead, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard V.
s: The worshippers of Mazda must raise three small houses for the dead in every house and borough when summer has passed and winter has come. Each must be large enough for a standing person to extend the feet and hands without striking the skull, feet, or hands.

l: Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard VI.
s: Ahura Mazda instructs Zarathustra on keeping ground fallow for a year after the death of dogs or men and on penalties for violating or failing to inspect it. He specifies penalties for placing bones or bodies on the ground, and procedures for removing corpses from ponds, wells, snow, hail, and running streams so the water can become clean. He explains how touched Haoma may be purified, where the dead and their bones should be placed, and how corpses must be secured against being carried to water or trees.

l: Ahura Mazda, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard VI.
s: Ahura Mazda answers Zarathustra’s questions about defiled ground, bones, corpses, water, Haoma, and the treatment of the dead. He prescribes purification procedures and penalties, including stripes with the Aspahê-astra and the Sraoshô-karana.

l: Zarathustra, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard VI.
s: Zarathustra is addressed by Ahura Mazda as the questioner concerning the required treatment of ground, water, Haoma, corpses, and bones.

l: worshippers of Mazda, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard VI.
s: Worshippers of Mazda must leave ground fallow for a year where dogs or men have died and must not sow or water it during that year. They must inspect the ground for bones, hair, flesh, dung, and blood, remove corpses from water, secure corpses against dispersal, and provide suitable places for bones.

l: Drug Nasu, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard VI.
s: Drug Nasu defiles parts of ponds, wells, snow or hail, and running water when a corpse is present. The extent of defilement and the means of purification are specified for each kind of water.

l: Haoma, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard VI.
s: Haoma touched by a corpse can be made clean again. If it has been strained for the Sacrifice, no corpse brought to it causes corruption or death; if it has not been strained, four fingers’ length of the stem must be buried for a year.

l: ground, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard VI.
s: Ground where dogs or men have died must lie fallow for a year and must not be sown or watered during that time. Before it is tilled again, it must be inspected for bones, hair, flesh, dung, and blood.

l: dog, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard VI.
s: Dogs are included among those whose deaths require the ground to lie fallow for a year. Dead dogs are also included in the bones and bodies whose placement on the ground incurs penalties.

l: men, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard VI.
s: Men are included among those whose deaths require the ground to lie fallow for a year. Dead men are also included in the bones and bodies whose placement on the ground incurs penalties.

l: corpse, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard VI.
s: A corpse found in running water must be removed and laid on dry ground, even when it is falling to pieces and rotting. Corpses in ponds, wells, snow or hail, and running streams render specified portions of water unclean until removed and the required purification is completed.

l: bones of the dead, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard VI.
s: Bones of dead dogs or men placed on the ground incur penalties that increase with their size, from thirty stripes to one thousand stripes with each of the two instruments. The bones of the dead should be kept in a building beyond the reach of dogs, foxes, and wolves and where rain-water cannot stay.

l: water, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard VI.
s: Water containing a corpse is unclean and unfit to drink until the corpse is removed. Depending on the water source, part of the water must be drawn off or the water must melt, flow, or pass through specified intervals before it becomes clean.

l: running stream, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard VI.
s: A corpse in a running stream defiles three steps down the stream, nine steps up the stream, and six steps across. After the corpse is removed and the stream has flowed three times, the water is clean.

l: building, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard VI.
s: A building for the bones of the dead should be beyond the reach of the dog, fox, and wolf and should not retain rain-water. It should be made with stones, mortar, and earth if the worshippers of Mazda can afford it.

l: high summits, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard VI.
s: The bodies of the dead should be brought to the highest summits where corpse-eating dogs and corpse-eating birds are always known to be present.

l: death of dogs or men, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard VI.
s: The death of dogs or men requires the ground where the death occurred to remain fallow for a year. Sowing or watering that ground within the year is treated as bringing dead matter to water, earth, and plants.

l: sowing and watering ground, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard VI.
s: Worshippers of Mazda may sow and water the rest of the ground as they like, but not the part where dogs or men have died until a year has passed. Sowing or watering the defiled part within the year incurs the status of Peshôtanus and severe stripes.

l: removal of corpses from water, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard VI.
s: A person who encounters a corpse in running water must remove it after taking off shoes and clothes and entering the water as deeply as necessary. If the corpse is rotting, the person must draw out as much as can be grasped with both hands and lay it on dry ground.

l: pollution and purification of water, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard VI.
s: Pollution by a corpse affects specified areas of ponds, snow or hail, and running streams, while wells remain unclean until the corpse is removed. Purification involves removing the corpse and drawing off part of the water, melting snow or hail, or allowing a stream to flow three times.

l: punishments, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard VI.
s: Punishments include stripes with the Aspahê-astra and the Sraoshô-karana. They range from thirty stripes with each instrument for a small bone to one thousand stripes with each instrument for a whole body, with two hundred stripes each for several other offenses.

l: burial and securing of the dead, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard VI.
s: The dead should be placed on high summits and fastened by the feet and hair with brass, stones, or lead so dogs and birds cannot carry bones to water or trees. Bones should then be kept in a suitable building, or, if that cannot be afforded, the dead man may be laid on the ground on a carpet and pillow, clothed with the light of heaven and beholding the sun.

l: Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard VII.
s: Fargard VII concerns the pollution caused by death and the rules for cleansing people, clothing, utensils, animals, wood, corn, and ground. Ahura Mazda tells Zarathustra when the Drug Nasu attacks the dead and how far its pollution extends. It also sets rules for healing, payments to healers, Dakhmas and fiends, the treatment of a woman with a still-born child, and offerings defiled by the dead.

l: Fargard VII, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard VII.
s: It sets out rules concerning the Drug Nasu, death pollution, cleansing, healing, Dakhmas, fiends, still-born children, and defiled offerings.

l: Zarathustra, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard VII.
s: He asks Ahura Mazda about death, pollution, cleansing, healing, Dakhmas, fiends, and the treatment of a woman with a still-born child.

l: Ahura Mazda, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard VII.
s: He explains when the Drug Nasu attacks, how pollution is cleansed, how healers qualify and are paid, how long ground remains polluted, and how a woman with a still-born child is treated.

l: Drug Nasu, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard VII.
s: She rushes upon a dead man after death, or at the next watch in certain cases, in the shape of a raging fly. She defiles nearby people, bedding, clothing, and other things, and attacks those who eat corpses or bring corpses with filth into water or fire.

l: dead man, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard VII.
s: After death, the Drug Nasu rushes upon him. His corpse pollutes nearby people and objects, while the ground beneath it may require a year or fifty years to become itself again, depending on whether it lies on the ground or is buried.

l: clothing, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard VII.
s: Clothing touched by a corpse can be cleansed with gômêz, earth, and water if it is not defiled with seed, sweat, dirt, or vomit. Cleansed clothing cannot be used by priests, warriors, or husbandmen, but may cover a sick woman or an unfit man.

l: gômêz, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard VII.
s: It is used with earth and water to cleanse clothing, wood, corn, eating vessels, a woman with a still-born child, and a cow that has eaten a corpse.

l: water, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard VII.
s: It is used in cleansing clothing, wood, corn, eating vessels, and a cow. Water brought into contact with a corpse is defiled, and a woman with a still-born child may drink it only to save her life with permission from a holy man.

l: fiends, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard VII.
s: They gather at Dakhmas where corpses are laid, feed and void filth there, and cause disease and other harmful conditions. Gainis strengthen diseases among people of evil spirit.

l: corpse, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard VII.
s: It can pollute wood and corn, which may be cleansed by setting them apart at prescribed distances and sprinkling them with water, depending on their condition.

l: worshippers of Mazda, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard VII.
s: They must follow the rules for cleansing, treatment of corpses, healing, and offerings. A healer may treat them with the knife only after proving his skill on worshippers of the Daêvas.

l: worshippers of the Daêvas, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard VII.
s: A healer must first test his skill on them. If he causes three of them to die, he becomes permanently unfit to practise healing; if he heals three, he becomes fit to practise it.

l: art of healing, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard VII.
s: A healer qualifies by successfully treating three worshippers of the Daêvas and becomes permanently unfit after causing three such patients to die. Healing with the holy word is said to drive away sickness best when compared with healing by the knife or herbs.

l: ground, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard VII.
s: Ground where a dead man's corpse lies becomes itself again after one year, while earth containing a buried corpse becomes itself again after fifty years. Ground beneath a Dakhma does not recover until the corpse's dust mingles with the earth.

l: Dakhma, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard VII.
s: A Dakhma is a place where corpses are laid and where fiends gather, feed, and cause pollution and disease. Ahura Mazda urges people to pull down Dakhmas, and says that doing so can remit sins.

l: woman with child, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard VII.
s: If she gives birth to a still-born child, she is placed in an enclosure thirty paces from the fire, water, and consecrated baresma, and three paces from the faithful. She remains there for three nights, follows a prescribed diet, and is then cleansed with gômêz and water.

l: still-born child, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard VII.
s: Its birth causes the woman with child to be treated as unclean and placed in a separate enclosure according to prescribed distances from fire, water, baresma, and the faithful.

l: Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard VIII.
s: Fargard VIII concerns the treatment of dogs and men who die, corpse pollution, purification, penalties, sexual conduct, and the law of Mazda. Ahura Mazda instructs the worshippers of Mazda where to place dead bodies, how to move them, how to purify people and places, and how to drive away the Drug Nasu. It also describes punishments for covering a dead body, rules concerning involuntary and voluntary emission of seed, and the cleansing power of confession under the law of Mazda. The unit identifies the Daêva through sexual acts between men and women and traces the Drug Nasu’s movement during ritual washing.

l: Fargard VIII, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard VIII.
s: Fargard VIII sets out rules concerning dead dogs and men, corpse removal, purification, ritual penalties, sexual conduct, and the law of Mazda. It includes instructions attributed to Ahura Mazda on dealing with the Drug Nasu and the Daêva.

l: Ahura Mazda, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard VIII.
s: Ahura Mazda answers questions about corpses, houses, graves, purification, penalties, sexual conduct, the law of Mazda, and the Daêva. He instructs the worshippers of Mazda how to remove dead bodies, cleanse the unclean, and drive away the Drug Nasu.

l: worshippers of Mazda, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard VIII.
s: The worshippers of Mazda must find a Dakhma, handle dead bodies according to prescribed conditions, perfume houses, dig graves, move corpses, and perform purification rites. They also recite or arrange for the recitation of fiend-smiting words and may later bring people, animals, Fire, baresma, and food into a purified house.

l: dog, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard VIII.
s: A dog that dies under a house or hut is treated like a dead body requiring removal and purification procedures. A yellow dog with four eyes or a white dog with yellow ears is led three, six, or nine times along a corpse-bearing way to drive away the Drug Nasu, and corpse-eating dogs may smite the Nasu on a corpse.

l: man, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard VIII.
s: A man who dies under a house or hut is removed or left while the house is treated according to the prescribed procedure. A man who touches a corpse may be purified under specified conditions, while penalties are imposed for placing clothes over a dead body or voluntarily emitting seed.

l: corpse, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard VIII.
s: A dead body is removed from a house when possible, or the house is removed while the body lies on the spot. It may remain in a grave for two nights, three nights, or a month until birds, plants, floods, and wind indicate that it can be carried to a corpse-bearing building.

l: house, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard VIII.
s: A house containing a dead dog or man is either left standing and perfumed or taken away, depending on which removal is easier. After prescribed purification, the house may be used for preparing meals with meat and wine and is said to be clean.

l: Dakhma, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard VIII.
s: The worshippers of Mazda are instructed to look for a Dakhma when a dog or man dies under a house or hut.

l: Fire, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard VIII.
s: Fire is called the son of Ahura Mazda and must be kept thirty paces from a grave prepared during adverse weather. A corpse-bearing way cannot initially be passed by Fire, but after the dog rite and recitation of fiend-smiting words, Fire may be brought through it.

l: water, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard VIII.
s: Water is kept thirty paces from a grave prepared in a house. It is used in purification after gômêz, and it is sprinkled over the body in a prescribed sequence from the skull to the feet.

l: grave, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard VIII.
s: A grave is dug in the cleanest, driest, and least-traveled place in the house when weather prevents immediate removal of the dead. It is half a foot deep in hard earth or half the height of a man in soft earth, and its surface is covered with ashes or cowdung and dust of bricks, stones, or dry earth.

l: building of clay, stones, and mortar, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard VIII.
s: The corpse-bearers carry the body to a building of clay, stones, and mortar on a place where corpse-eating dogs and birds are always found.

l: gômêz, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard VIII.
s: Urine of sheep or oxen is used by corpse-bearers to wash their hair and bodies, while urine of man or woman is excluded except that of the nearest kinsman or nearest kinswoman of the dead. Gômêz is also used in purification before water is applied.

l: Drug Nasu, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard VIII.
s: The Drug Nasu is described as flying away to the north in the shape of a stained, raging fly when a suitable dog is led along a corpse-bearing way. During purification it rushes from one body part to another as water reaches each place, finally leaving through the toes and soles toward the north.

l: fiend-smiting words, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard VIII.
s: Fiend-smiting words are recited aloud by an Âthravan before a corpse-bearing way is used and at the completion of purification. They invoke the will of the Lord, protection by Mazda, the smiting of the fiend, and the driving away of the Drug.

l: Drug, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard VIII.
s: The Drug is commanded to perish, rush away, and go to the regions of the north so that it may never again give the living world of the holy spirit to death. The fiend-smiting words are used against it.

l: law of Mazda, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard VIII.
s: The law of Mazda removes the bonds of sin from one who confesses it and resolves not to repeat forbidden deeds. It is said to remove or cleanse sins including breach of trust, murdering one of the faithful, burying a corpse, deeds without atonement, and every evil thought, word, and deed.

l: sin, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard VIII.
s: Sin may be removed through confession under the law of Mazda for a person who is not a professor of that law or has not been taught in it. The law is said to remove any sin that may be sinned, while voluntary emission of seed is described as a deed for which there is no atonement for those subject to the stated rule.

l: atonement, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard VIII.
s: There is no atonement for a man who voluntarily emits his seed when he is a professor of the law of Mazda or has been taught in it. For one who confesses sin under the law of Mazda, a full atonement is effected by means of that law.

l: cleansing, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard VIII.
s: Cleansing is performed through gômêz and water, with prescribed stages and bodily washing after contact with a corpse. The law of Mazda also cleanses the faithful from every evil thought, word, and deed.

l: Daêva, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Fargard VIII.
s: A man who lies with mankind as man lies with womankind, or as woman lies with mankind, is identified as a Daêva, a worshipper and paramour of the Daêvas, and a Daêva in his inmost self and whole being. He is described as becoming one of the unseen Daêvas after death.

l: Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, VIII.
s: Ahura Mazda instructs worshippers of Mazda how to deal with a corpse-burning fire, including killing the man responsible, removing the cauldron and tripod, and dispersing the fire. The text assigns rewards for bringing different kinds of fire to the Dâityô-gâtu, measured in fire-brands. It explains how a man who has touched a corpse may be cleansed using gômêz, water, running, and assistance from others. It also prescribes penalties and atonements involving water, trees, the Aspahê-astra, and the Sraoshô-karana.

l: Ahura Mazda, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, VIII.
s: Ahura Mazda answers questions about corpse-burning fire, rewards for bringing fires to the Dâityô-gâtu, and cleansing after touching a corpse. He prescribes the required actions, rewards, penalties, and atonements.

l: dead man, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, VIII.
s: A corpse is being burned or roasted on a corpse-burning fire. A man who has touched a corpse can be cleansed under the stated procedures.

l: corpse-burning fire, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, VIII.
s: A corpse-burning fire must be dealt with by killing the man who burns the corpse, removing the cauldron and tripod, and dispersing the fire in successive bundles. Its fire may also be brought to the Dâityô-gâtu, where it receives the reward of ten thousand fire-brands.

l: Fire, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, VIII.
s: Fire, the son of Ahura Mazda, goes wherever the perfume of certain sweet-smelling woods is carried by the wind and kills thousands of unseen Daêvas, fiends, Yâtus, and Pairikas.

l: Dâityô-gâtu, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, VIII.
s: The Dâityô-gâtu is the destination to which various fires may be brought. The rewards are measured as equivalent to specified numbers of fire-brands, depending on the kind of fire brought.

l: fire-brands, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, VIII.
s: Fire-brands measure the posthumous rewards for bringing fires to the Dâityô-gâtu. The stated equivalents range from ten thousand for a corpse-burning fire to ten for a man's own hearth fire.

l: Drug Nasu, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, VIII.
s: Nasu is treated as having been or not having been smitten by corpse-eating dogs or birds. This condition determines whether the man who touched the corpse must wash thirty times or fifteen times.

l: gômêz, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, VIII.
s: Gômêz is used to wash the body of a man who has touched a corpse. The man uses it before rubbing himself dry and, if cleansing by others is unavailable, uses it with water.

l: water, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, VIII.
s: Water is used with gômêz to cleanse a man who has touched a corpse when others will not cleanse him. If he finds water on his way, the water requires atonement, for which he must receive the stated penalty.

l: man who has touched a corpse, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, VIII.
s: A man who has touched a corpse without wilful sin must wash with gômêz, rub himself dry, run specified distances, and call out that he wishes to be made clean. If no one cleanses him, he may cleanse himself with gômêz and water, but he incurs penalties when he finds water or trees on the way.

l: Aspahê-astra, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, VIII.
s: The Aspahê-astra is used in the prescribed atonement of four hundred stripes when the man who touched a corpse finds water or trees on his way.

l: Sraoshô-karana, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, VIII.
s: The Sraoshô-karana is used in the prescribed atonement of four hundred stripes when the man who touched a corpse finds water or trees on his way.

l: the burning of corpses, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, VIII.
s: Corpse burning is condemned through the command to kill the man who burns the corpse. The corpse-burning fire must have its cauldron and tripod removed and must be dispersed so that it dies out sooner.

l: bringing fire to the Dâityô-gâtu, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, VIII.
s: Bringing fire to the Dâityô-gâtu earns a reward after the man's soul has parted from his body. The reward varies according to the fire, from ten thousand fire-brands for corpse-burning fire to ten for the fire of his own hearth.

l: cleansing after touching a corpse, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, VIII.
s: Cleansing after touching a corpse involves washing with gômêz, rubbing dry, running until meeting or overtaking others, and calling aloud for cleansing. If others refuse, the man ultimately cleanses himself with gômêz and water.

l: atonement, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII, VIII.
s: Atonement is required when the man who touched a corpse finds water or trees on his way. The stated atonement is four hundred stripes with the Aspahê-astra and four hundred stripes with the Sraoshô-karana.

l: Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard IX.
s: Fargard IX concerns the nine-night Barashnûm, a ritual for cleansing a person defiled by the dead. Zarathustra asks Ahura Mazda how the cleansing should be performed, and Ahura Mazda describes the prepared ground, holes, furrows, sprinkling, washing, recitations, and periods of seclusion. The unit also sets rewards for those who cleanse others, penalties for those who perform the rites without knowing them, and the consequences for the material world. It teaches that the Drug Nasu is driven away by proper cleansing and that sweetness, health, and growth return only after an Ashemaogha is killed and Sraosha is offered sacrifice for three days and three nights.

l: Fargard IX, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard IX.
s: Fargard IX sets out the nine-night Barashnûm, including its ritual procedures, rewards, penalties, and consequences for those defiled by the dead.

l: Barashnûm, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard IX.
s: The Barashnûm is a cleansing rite lasting nine nights for one defiled by the dead. It involves holes, furrows, gômêz, water, recitations, washing, and periods of seclusion.

l: Zarathustra, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard IX.
s: Zarathustra asks Ahura Mazda about cleansing the body of one defiled by the dead and how to fight the Drug Nasu. He is instructed to recite and oversee the cleansing rites.

l: Ahura Mazda, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard IX.
s: Ahura Mazda explains the rites of cleansing, the required distances and measurements, the actions against the Drug Nasu, the rewards for cleansers, and the penalties for improper cleansing.

l: godly man, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard IX.
s: A godly man who speaks truth, learns the Holy Word, and knows the rites of cleansing according to the law of Mazda may prepare the ground and perform the cleansing.

l: unclean one, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard IX.
s: The unclean one walks to the holes, is sprinkled with gômêz, cleanses the body with dust, washes with water, and remains secluded for three, six, and nine nights. After nine nights and a final washing, the unclean one may approach the fire, water, earth, cow, trees, and faithful.

l: faithful, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard IX.
s: The faithful must be kept at a distance from the cleansing ground and from the unclean one during the periods of seclusion. The faithful are pleased when someone is properly cleansed from the Nasu.

l: worshippers of Mazda, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard IX.
s: The worshippers of Mazda give cattle or another suitable reward to the person who cleanses them, if they can afford it. They must bind and punish one who performs cleansing without knowing the rites according to the law of Mazda.

l: Nasu, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard IX.
s: The Drug Nasu moves over the unclean one's body from the head toward the feet as gômêz is sprinkled. She is driven to the toes and then flies north in the shape of a raging fly; improper cleansing makes her stronger.

l: Drug, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard IX.
s: The Drug becomes weaker at the words that smite Angra Mainyu, Aêshma, the Mâzainya fiends, and all the fiends. The Drug is also said to fade away when the prescribed Gâthic words are recited.

l: Ashemaogha, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard IX.
s: Ashemaogha is the ungodly person who cleanses the unclean without knowing the rites according to the law of Mazda. Until Ashemaogha is put to death, sweetness, health, healing, fulness, increase, and growth do not return to the affected land and fields.

l: Sraosha, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard IX.
s: Sraosha must be offered a sacrifice in the affected place for three days and three nights, with fire blazing, baresma tied up, and Haoma uplifted, after Ashemaogha has been put to death.

l: material world, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard IX.
s: The material world is threatened with loss of fulness and increase and with the arrival of sickness and death when cleansing is performed improperly.

l: Fire, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard IX.
s: Fire is identified as the son of Ahura Mazda and must be kept thirty paces from the cleansing ground. The unclean one must avoid Fire during the nine nights of seclusion and may approach it afterward.

l: water, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard IX.
s: Water must be thirty paces from the cleansing ground. The unclean one washes at the first hole once, at the second twice, and at the third three times, while avoiding water during seclusion.

l: gômêz, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard IX.
s: Gômêz is sprinkled over the unclean one from a brass or lead spoon attached to a nine-knotted stick. It is also used with water to clean the body and clothes after each period of seclusion.

l: nine holes, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard IX.
s: The cleansing ground contains six holes followed by three more, dug to seasonal depths and placed at specified distances. The unclean one approaches them, uses them during sprinkling, and washes at the first three holes.

l: furrow, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard IX.
s: A metal knife is used to draw furrows around the holes. Twelve furrows are made, with stones, potsherds, stumps, clods, or other hard matter placed as steps at the specified intervals.

l: Yathâ ahû vairyô, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard IX.
s: Yathâ ahû vairyô is among the fiend-smiting and most-healing words recited during the cleansing. It is recited when the Drug Nasu is driven away and at each of the six holes.

l: the cleansing ritual, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard IX.
s: The rites of cleansing require knowledge of the law of Mazda and include preparing the ground, reciting words, sprinkling with gômêz, using dust and water, applying perfumes, and observing nine nights of seclusion.

l: defilement by the dead, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard IX.
s: Defilement by the dead is cleansed through the Barashnûm. A person defiled by the dead is considered dangerous to the purity of the world until the prescribed cleansing and seclusion are completed.

l: cleansing, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard IX.
s: Proper cleansing delights the sun, moon, stars, fire, water, earth, cow, trees, and faithful. Its reward for the cleanser in the other world is the welfare of the blessed abode.

l: sickness and death, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard IX.
s: Sickness and death become stronger when a person who does not know the rites performs the cleansing. They threaten the land and fields until the improper cleanser is put to death and the required sacrifice to Sraosha is performed.

l: Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard X.
s: Zarathustra asks Ahura Mazda how to fight the Drug that rushes from the dead upon the living and defiles them. Ahura Mazda instructs him to recite specified words in the Gâthas twice, thrice, or four times, followed by fiend-smiting and most-healing words that drive away various fiends and defilements. He commands Zarathustra to dig nine holes in a dry, sparsely wooded part of the ground and teaches that purity is the greatest good next to life. Purity can be won by cleansing oneself with good thoughts, words, and deeds according to the law of Mazda.

l: Zarathustra, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard X.
s: Zarathustra asks Ahura Mazda how to fight the Drug that comes from the dead and defiles the living. He is instructed to recite specified Gâthas and other fiend-smiting and most-healing words, and to dig nine holes in a suitable part of the ground.

l: Ahura Mazda, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard X.
s: Ahura Mazda answers Zarathustra's questions and prescribes recitations from the Gâthas to be said twice, thrice, or four times. He also gives words for driving away fiends and defilement and teaches the requirements for purity.

l: Drug, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard X.
s: The Drug is described as rushing from the dead upon the living and defiling the living. The prescribed words are said to stand against it.

l: Angra Mainyu, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard X.
s: Angra Mainyu is driven away by the prescribed words from the house, borough, town, land, the bodies of those defiled by the dead, their leaders, and the whole holy world. The words are also said to smite down Angra Mainyu.

l: Nasu, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard X.
s: Nasu is driven away by the prescribed words from the house, borough, town, land, the bodies of those defiled by the dead, their leaders, and the whole holy world. It is identified as the defilement that rushes from the dead upon the living.

l: Gâthas, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard X.
s: The Gâthas contain words that are to be recited twice, thrice, or four times aloud. Specific passages from the Gâthas are listed for each number of repetitions.

l: house, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard X.
s: The house is among the places from which Angra Mainyu, Nasu, direct and indirect defilement, and various fiends are driven away.

l: borough, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard X.
s: The borough is among the places from which Angra Mainyu, Nasu, direct and indirect defilement, and various fiends are driven away.

l: town, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard X.
s: The town is among the places from which Angra Mainyu, Nasu, direct and indirect defilement, and various fiends are driven away.

l: land, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard X.
s: The land is among the places from which Angra Mainyu, Nasu, direct and indirect defilement, and various fiends are driven away.

l: holy world, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard X.
s: The whole holy world is included among the places and beings from which Angra Mainyu, Nasu, defilement, and various fiends are driven away.

l: dead, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard X.
s: The dead are the source from which the Drug and Nasu rush upon and defile the living.

l: living, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard X.
s: The living are threatened by the Drug and Nasu, which rush from the dead and defile them. The final prayer asks that the living world no longer be given to death.

l: purity, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard X.
s: Purity is described as the greatest good for man next to life. It is obtained through the law of Mazda by cleansing oneself with good thoughts, words, and deeds.

l: law of Mazda, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard X.
s: The law of Mazda procures purity for the person who cleanses himself with good thoughts, words, and deeds.

l: good thoughts, good words, and good deeds, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard X.
s: Good thoughts, words, and deeds are the means by which a person cleanses himself and wins purity.

l: Ke verethrem gâ, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard X.
s: The fiend-smiting and most-healing words are recited after the specified Gâthas. They drive away Angra Mainyu, Nasu, defilement, Indra, Sauru, Naunghaithya, Tauru, Zairi, Aêshma, Akatasha, the Varenya daêvas, and the wind-daêva.

l: purification, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard X.
s: Purification requires digging nine holes in the part of the ground where there is least water and where there are fewest trees, with nothing there that may be food for man or beast. A person can achieve purification by cleansing himself with good thoughts, words, and deeds.

l: Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard XI.
s: Zarathustra asks Ahura Mazda how to cleanse the house, fire, water, earth, cow, tree, faithful people, celestial bodies, boundless light, and all good things made by Mazda. Ahura Mazda answers that cleansing is performed by chanting cleansing words, including repeated Ahuna-Vairyas, Mazdâ ad môi, and Airyama-ishyô. The words drive away Aêshma, the Nasu, defilements, several named demons, the Pairika, the demon of uncleanness, and Angra Mainyu. The unit teaches that the law of holiness and the prescribed chants protect and purify the material world and its inhabitants.

l: Zarathustra, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard XI.
s: Zarathustra asks Ahura Mazda how to cleanse the house, fire, water, earth, cow, tree, faithful people, the stars, the moon, the sun, boundless light, and all good things made by Mazda.

l: Ahura Mazda, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard XI.
s: Ahura Mazda instructs Zarathustra to chant cleansing words to make the house, fire, water, earth, cow, tree, faithful people, celestial bodies, boundless light, and all good things clean. He prescribes repeated Ahuna-Vairyas, Mazdâ ad môi, and Airyama-ishyô, and teaches words that drive away fiends and Angra Mainyu.

l: Angra Mainyu, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard XI.
s: Angra Mainyu is called mischievous and is driven away from the fire, water, earth, cow, tree, faithful man, faithful woman, stars, moon, sun, boundless light, and all good things made by Mazda.

l: Drug, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard XI.
s: Drug is commanded to perish and rush away to the regions of the north, never again giving the living world of the holy spirit unto death.

l: Aêshma of the bloody spear, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard XI.
s: The fiend is opposed by fiend-smiting and most-healing words. The chants ask who will smite the fiend, command the fiend to perish, and drive away the brood and world of the fiend.

l: house, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard XI.
s: The house is cleansed by saying aloud, "He is my greatest support as long as lasts this dreary world."

l: Fire, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard XI.
s: The fire is cleansed by saying aloud, "Thy fire, first of all, do we approach with worship, O Ahura Mazda!" Pairika and the demon of uncleanness that come upon the fire are driven away.

l: water, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard XI.
s: The water is cleansed by worshipping the waters in the tree, stream, and rain. Pairika and the demon of uncleanness that come upon the water are driven away.

l: earth, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard XI.
s: The earth is cleansed by worshipping the earth with the women, which bears people and those women who are Ahura's. Pairika and the demon of uncleanness that come upon the earth are driven away.

l: cow, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard XI.
s: The cow is cleansed through words ordering excellent deeds so that she may have a resting place and fodder. Pairika and the demon of uncleanness that come upon the cow are driven away.

l: trees, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard XI.
s: The trees are cleansed by saying that Mazda made the plants grow through holiness. Pairika and the demon of uncleanness that come upon the tree are driven away.

l: faithful man, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard XI.
s: The faithful man is cleansed by calling the beloved Airyaman for the men and women of Zarathustra to rejoice, with the desirable reward won by means of the law and the boon for holiness vouchsafed by Ahura.

l: the faithful woman, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard XI.
s: The faithful woman is cleansed by calling the beloved Airyaman for the men and women of Zarathustra to rejoice, with the desirable reward won by means of the law and the boon for holiness vouchsafed by Ahura.

l: all good things made by Mazda, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard XI.
s: All good things made by Mazda, the offspring of the holy principle, are included among the things cleansed by the prescribed words. Angra Mainyu and the forces of uncleanness are driven away from them.

l: holy principle, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard XI.
s: The holy principle is identified as the source of all good things made by Mazda. The chants seek to preserve and cleanse what is connected with it.

l: cleansing, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard XI.
s: Cleansing is performed through prescribed spoken words and repeated chants. It makes the named parts of the material world clean and drives away fiends, defilements, demons, and Angra Mainyu.

l: Ke verethrem gâ, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard XI.
s: The cleansing words are described as fiend-smiting and most-healing. They include the Ahuna-Vairya, Mazdâ ad môi, Airyama-ishyô, words for particular objects, and formulas driving away uncleanness.

l: Ahuna-Vairya, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard XI.
s: The Ahuna-Vairya is chanted five times, eight times, four times, and five times at different stages of the cleansing. Its words include the statement, "The will of the Lord is the law of holiness," and it is said to preserve the person of man.

l: the law of holiness, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard XI.
s: The law of holiness is identified with the will of the Lord. The text connects it with protection, cleansing, the desirable reward, and the works through which the world may thrive.

l: Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard XII.
s: Fargard XII. concerns the periods of mourning required after the death of relatives and the cleansing of the house afterward. Ahura Mazda states that the required stays range from thirty or sixty days for parents and children to six months or a year for the master or mistress of the house, with shorter periods for more distant relatives. The house is cleansed by washing bodies and clothes, chanting the Gâthas, offering sacrifice and baresma, and bringing libations to the good waters before the waters, fire, and Amesha-Spentas may enter. Ahura Mazda also teaches that a dead stranger who did not profess the true faith no longer directly or indirectly defiles creation, unlike the living Ashemaogha.

l: Fargard XII., Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard XII.
s: Fargard XII. sets out mourning periods for deaths among relatives and explains how the house is to be cleansed afterward. It also discusses the defilement caused by a living Ashemaogha and the lack of such defilement after his death.

l: Ahura Mazda, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard XII.
s: Ahura Mazda answers Spitama Zarathustra's questions about mourning, house cleansing, and defilement. He prescribes the mourning periods and cleansing actions, and teaches that a dead stranger no longer defiles the creation of the good spirit.

l: Zarathustra, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard XII.
s: Spitama Zarathustra receives Ahura Mazda's instructions concerning mourning, the cleansing of the house, and the defilement caused by the living Ashemaogha.

l: Ashemaogha, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard XII.
s: The living Ashemaogha directly defiles the creatures of the good spirit and indirectly defiles them. While alive, he smites water, blows out fire, carries off the cow, kills the faithful man, and deprives him of food, clothing, house, bed, and vessels; when dead, he no longer does these things.

l: mourning for the dead, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard XII.
s: Mourning lasts thirty days for the righteous and sixty days for sinners after the death of a parent or child; six months or a year after the death of the master or mistress of the house; and progressively shorter periods for more distant relatives. The stated periods are twenty-five or fifty days for grandparents and grandchildren, twenty or forty days for uncles or aunts, fifteen or thirty days for cousins, ten or twenty days for a cousin's child, and five or ten days for a cousin's grandchild.

l: death, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard XII.
s: Death determines the period of mourning and requires the house to be cleansed before the waters, fire, and Amesha-Spentas may enter. The death of a stranger who does not profess the true faith does not directly or indirectly defile creation in the way the living Ashemaogha does.

l: house, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard XII.
s: The house becomes clean after the prescribed washing, chanting, offerings, and libations. Once cleansed, the waters, fire, and Amesha-Spentas may enter it.

l: cleansing, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard XII.
s: Cleansing the house requires washing the bodies three times, washing the clothes three times, chanting the Gâthas three times, offering a sacrifice to the Fire, offering the bundles of baresma, and bringing libations to the good waters.

l: stranger, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargard XII.
s: A stranger who dies without professing the true faith or true law directly or indirectly defiles the creation of the good spirit no more than a dead frog whose venom is dried up and which has been dead more than a year.
